newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Gulf War hero Powell backs US arms sales to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War hero Powell backs US arms sales to Taiwan.

text.p: Retired U.S. military chief Colin Powell said on Monday he believed Washington would not change its policy of ensuring Taiwan's supply of defensive weapons.
Powell, said by some to be considering a run for the U.S. presidency in 2000, told reporters in Taipei that it was in the United States' interest to help Taiwan maintain adequate defences.
"I think what we do necessarily is to make sure that Taiwan has proper self-defence," said Powell, who was chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff under President George Bush.
"That's what I did when I was chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and I know that it will continue to be the U.S. policy," he said.
Powell said Washington's policy of arming Nationalist-ruled Taiwan over communist China's protests was correct.

"I think we've got a very satisfactory arms sales policy, which is to make sure and allow Taiwanese to be safe and secure, and strengthen their own arms or strengthen their defence," the 59-year-old retired general said.
Taiwan is preparing to take delivery of 150 U.S.-made F-16 fighters and installing batteries of the U.S. Patriot antimissile missile made famous during the 1991 Gulf War overseen by Powell.

He described Taiwan-U.S. ties as "excellent," citing Washington's dispatch of two aircraft carrier groups to the region in March last year as a counterweight to intimidating war games and missile tests being mounted at the time by Beijing.
Powell said the U.S. move was stabilising, not provocative.

Beijing launched eight months of military manoeuvres near Taiwan after the island's president, Lee Teng-hui, made a private visit to New York -- a journey China interpreted as an attempt to promote Taiwan's independence.
China has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949 and has warned other countries not to forge diplomatic ties or sell arms to Taiwan.
Powell, began a two-day visit on Monday, said in a speech that he would try to ensure that Taiwan's security "remains the No.1 priority for the United States."
Powell met Premier Lien Chan and Foreign Minister John Chang and showed up at a bookstore to sign copies of a Chinese translation of his autobiography, "My American Journey."
The state-funded Central News Agency quoted Lien as urging Washington to continue to supply Taiwan with defensive arms to counter China's military modernisation.
"Based on continued weapons expansion by the Chinese communists, we need continued arms supplies from the United States," Lien was quoted as saying.
